sect1.title: Setting up procmail
sect1.para: When postfix receives a mail it will by default store the mail in the mail spool directory (either “/var/spool/mail/user” or “/var/mail/user”).

Postfix offers no possibility of post-processing of the received mails. For example to run the received mails through a spamfilter (like spamassassin) and put all identified spams in a separate mail folder.

To solve this we tell postfix to send all the received mails that should be locally delivered through another program, in our case procmail. It is this program that will act as a Local Delivery Agent, LDA, and perform the last stage when incoming mails are store on disk.

sect2.title: Configuration file
sect2.para: Procmail is controlled with (yet another) configuration file which by default is in the home directory of the user receiving the mail .procmailrc) . The configuration file will contain rules on how to process the incoming mails, such as storing mails based on different criteria in different folders. It is even possible to have certain mails automatically trigger other external programs. A typical use of this would be a server where users can send a one line mail to have some useful information automatically sent back.
In order to tell postfix to send incoming mails to procmail we must add the following line in the postfix config file (/etc/postfix/main.cf)

The next step is to setup the configuration file for procmail. Since it is possible to write an entire book on how to write procmail filtering rule we will keep this example simple. The example rule file below will do the following:

listitem.para: we will enable logging in a separate log file for each user under the /tmp directory
if the mail is judged to be “normal” spam we store it in the folder “Junk”
if the mail have a very high spam score we just discard them by deleting them forever
if the mail has the word “Newsletter” in the subject or comes from a sender “*.news.com” we put it in a separate mail folder “Newsletters”
otherwise we store it in the default inbox

sect2.para: The home page for procmail has many more receipts that you can take directly. For example “Out of office” style of automatic replies.

Unfortunately the syntax for procmail configuration is not exactly intuitive (anyone who think that has spent too much time with mail servers) but the basic structure in this example file will get you a good start and will serve a good start for your own experiments. It would bring this tutorial too far off track to become a “How To Write procmail Filter rules” as well. Refer to the procmail documentation for details.

Don't be discouraged if procmail's syntax seems cryptic at first. The learning curve is steep, but the example configurations provided should cover most common needs. Start with the simple filtering rules shown here and add complexity gradually as you become comfortable. When troubleshooting procmail rules, the log file (specified with LOGFILE in your configuration) is invaluable - it shows exactly which rules matched and where each mail ended up. If a rule isn't working as expected, first check the log to see if the rule is being triggered at all.
In we also show some more example of procmail configuration recipes.

example.title: Template for a procmail configuration file
example.programlisting:
#--------------------------------------------- # Standard setup for extra logging #--------------------------------------------- VERBOSE=on LOGABSTRACT=all LOGFILE=/tmp/procmail-${LOGNAME}-`date +%Y%m`.log MAILDIR=/srv/mail/${LOGNAME} DEFAULT=${MAILDIR}/ INBOX=${MAILDIR}/
#--------------------------------------------- # Subfolders to filter mails in. # REMEMBER TO PUT TRAILING '/' AT # THE END # to mark the folders as being in maildir format #--------------------------------------------- SPAM=${MAILDIR}/.Junk/ NEWSLETTERS=${MAILDIR}/.newsletters/
##-------------------------------------------- ## End of setup. Now comes all the filer ## rules. ##--------------------------------------------
#--------------------------------------------- # FILTER for Newsletters. #--------------------------------------------- :0 ^Subject:.*Newsletter ^From:.*news.com { } :0 E $NEWSLETTERS
#--------------------------------------------- # FILTER for spamassassin #--------------------------------------------- :0 * < 512000 | /usr/bin/spamc #--------------------------------------------- # Discard all spams with score >= 15 #--------------------------------------------- :0 * !^X-Spam-Level: \*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*.* * !^X-Spam-Status: Yes, score=1[5-9]\.[0-9] * !^X-Spam-Status: Yes, score=[2-9][0-9]\.[0-9] { } :0 E /dev/null
#--------------------------------------------- # Put all remaining spams in Junk folder. # NOTE: This assumes spamassassin is configured # to set the X-Spam-Flag: YES for identified # spams. #--------------------------------------------- :0 * ^X-Spam-Flag: YES $SPAM
#--------------------------------------------- # Send the remaing mails to the inbox #--------------------------------------------- :0 $DEFAULT

note.para: By default procmail only supports “AND” rules, i.e. if you add a number of conditions before an action all of them has to be fulfilled for the action to be performed.
One of the most frequent questions newcomers to procmail have is therefore how to write “OR” rules, i.e. a rule that states that

para.code: if condition1 or condition2 is true then do action

note.para: The way around this is to realize that

para.code: “if A or B then do C”
“if (not A) and (not B) then do nothing else do C”.

note.para: Any book on Boolean logic will give more details on this subject.
